newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pork exports to surge after Taiwan hog epidemic.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pork exports to surge after Taiwan hog epidemic.

text.p: U.S. pork exports are expected to surge this year as a result of a devastating hog epidemic in Taiwan that has crippled herds on the island and forced an export ban.

The U.S. Agriculture Department Friday sharply raised its 1997 export forecast for U.S. pork to 1.365 billion pounds, up from last month's estimate of 1.110 billion and well above last year's exports of 951 million pounds.
"The United States is expected to gain the lion's share of fresh product that Taiwan would have exported and part of the frozen product market," the department said.
Last month Taiwan banned exports and ordered a mass slaughter of 2 million pigs after confirming an outbreak of the deadly, contagious foot-and-mouth disease.

Analysts had been predicting that the U.S. pork industry would get a shot in the arm from Taiwan's hog woes. Agriculture Department General Sales Manager Chris Goldthwait said last month there likely would be commercial opportunites for U.S. pork in Taiwan's traditional pork markets.
The hog epidemic has wiped out the island's huge exports to Japan. Taiwan had provided 45 percent of Japan's pork imports, while the United States accounted for 23 percent.

For the U.S. producers, it may be a double-edged sword. Taiwan has long been a top customer for U.S. corn and soybeans and demand is seen tapering off due to the hog crisis. Rising U.S. pork shipments could help offset the loss of corn and soybean exports to the country, analysts say.
Analysts have said the epidemic could shave as much as one percentage point off Taiwan's gross domestic product growth in 1997.
